extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature; general readers interested in Shakespearean criticism and theatre history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical standards for assessing Shakespeare's authorship, textual status, stage performance, and literary merits across historical critical schools (neoclassical, romantic, historical, textual scholarship).

rubrics_metrics.name: External evidence for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays 'appeared under his name during his lifetime' and were 'acted by his company' — such external facts (title-pages, registrations, performance records) are cited as evidence of Shakespeare's authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include Pericles, The London Prodigal, and A Yorkshire Tragedy; but the text cautions that title-page attributions can be 'a bookseller's mistake or deception without warrant.' External evidence should therefore be weighed carefully and corroborated with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse and stylistic tests for attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Various verse tests and stylistic analyses are used to assign portions of plays to particular authors (e.g., assigning about two fifths of The Two Noble Kinsmen to Shakespeare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites specific scene-assignments as evidence (I. i; I. ii; etc.). Such metrical/verse tests are presented as confirming aesthetic judgment but are used alongside other lines of evidence rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward late or bookseller attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many plays were ascribed to Shakespeare by late seventeenth-century booksellers or in catalogs without grounds; such attributions often lack warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles like The Merry Devil of Edmonton, The Arraignment of Paris, Fair Em, Mucedorus, and The Birth of Merlin are cited as examples; caution is urged when relying solely on post hoc or commercial attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and evaluation of forgeries
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgeries of documents and manuscripts (e.g., by Ireland and Collier) have been produced purporting to relate to Shakespeare and can vitiate scholarship if accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts exposures (Ireland exposed by Malone; Collier's forgeries) and warns that forged manuscripts and fabricated papers can mislead research; scholars should validate provenance and authenticity of documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of cipher-based Baconian claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to find ciphers in the First Folio (to prove Baconian authorship) are 'mutually destructive' or require arbitrary manipulation and are therefore invalid as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works cited include The Great Cryptogram (Donnelly) and The Bi-Literal Cypher (Mrs. Gallup); the essay notes such cyphers either do not work without arbitrary choices or produce absurd results (pointing to authorship across impossible dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary and contextual corrective considerations for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of corrective considerations supports Shakespeare's authorship: records of his life are fuller than for other dramatists; identity between actor and writer is established; plays show practical actorly knowledge; extensive observation exists without signs of thorough scholarship; law-terms are common but explainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay enumerates these points to counter skepticism: (1) comparatively fuller records, (2) records linking actor and writer, (3) actorly diction and references, (4) wide observation not implying scholarly training, (5) plausible acquisition of legal terms. These serve as criteria to weigh claims denying authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neo-classical critical standards (unity, poetic justice, regularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century critics objected to irregularity and confusion of structure, the disregard of the unities of action, mixing of tragic and comic elements, lack of poetic justice, and insufficient didactic/moral purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rymer's demand for 'rationalized' tragedy and poetic justice is given as an explicit standard; these criteria were used to criticize Shakespeare's plots, characters, and dramatic effects and reflect the classical/rationalist ideals of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific stylistic criticisms: diction and rhetorical faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics charged Shakespeare with 'obscurity and archaism of diction, mixed and confused figures, occasional puns and bombast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are listed as recurring objections (e.g., Dryden and Rymer). Such stylistic faults were judged against contemporary taste and rhetorical norms and served as negative criteria in past critical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic/esthetic appreciative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic criticism valued Shakespeare's imaginative power: treating characters 'as if they were real persons,' emphasizing individuality, poetic imagination, emotion over reason, and finding in his work a synthetic philosophy or moral wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge, Schlegel, Goethe, and others exemplify this approach. The standard involves deep sympathetic interpretation, expansion of character (biographical reading), and seeking overarching aesthetic or ethical meaning rather than testing by formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual scholarship and criteria for establishing a sound text
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly work aims to establish a sound text and reliable chronology through careful collation, emendation, and editorial method; this is a continuing scholarly responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites Malone, Dyce, Ward, Fleay, and others; it emphasizes the role of editions (Rowe onward), the variorum tradition, and the eventual need to 'restrict, simplify, and finally determine' editorial practices. A sound text is measured by documentary support and consistent editorial principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-fidelity versus adaptive revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically plays were adapted to contemporary tastes (e.g., Nahum Tate's King Lear, Cibber's Richard III), but there is a modern preference for adherence to an authorized text and for performances closer to original Elizabethan practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptations are acknowledged as evidence of admiration but are criticized for distorting Shakespeare; Garrick is credited with restoring texts to the stage despite garbling, and more recent sentiment favors faithful texts rather than heavy revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting and interpretive performance as evaluative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors and acting styles (declamatory dignity vs. passionate vehemence) significantly shape the interpretation and reception of Shakespeare's plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Garrick, Kemble, Mrs. Siddons, Kean, Macready, Irving, Ellen Terry, Edwin Booth, etc.) illustrate how performers' approaches alter appreciation and influence which plays are revived and how they are understood; strong performances can renew interest and shape critical opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual criticism (Elizabethan situating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying Shakespeare as a sixteenth-century dramatist in relation to his time, theater, and literary environment is a criterion for understanding development, causes, and meaning of his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'historical criticism' combines documentary research (legal and court records, theatrical history) with knowledge of Elizabethan practices; it seeks to explain qualities of Shakespeare's achievement historically rather than by imposing later aesthetic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of influence (editions, performances, translations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's influence can be gauged empirically by the number and variety of editions, stage performances, translations, and adaptations across nations and centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay points to the multiplication of editions, the spread of translations (e.g., German translations and performance statistics), and the frequent acting of plays as indicators of influence; these are used as metrics in evaluating his cultural reach and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in assigning anonymous plays to a single author
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution of anonymous or collaborative plays to Shakespeare often relies on a few characteristic passages and may neglect that many contemporaries shared versification and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Arden of Feversham, Edward III, Sir Thomas More. The text warns that early in his career Shakespeare's style had not fully individualized, so similarity alone provides weak warrant for attribution without further corroboration.
